title: Execution Context and Scope
summary: Every line of JS runs inside an execution context built in two phases, and variable lookup walks a scope chain outward from it. Hoisting, the TDZ, and the classic loop bug all fall out of this one mechanism.

slides.markdown:
"What does this log?" is the single most common way a JS interview opens, and almost every version of it is really asking one question: **do you understand execution contexts and the scope chain?**

An execution context is the environment your code runs in — what variables exist, what `this` refers to, where an unresolved name should be looked up next. JavaScript builds one **before running a single statement**, in two distinct phases, and that two-phase build is exactly why `var` seems to "move to the top" of a function while `let` throws if you touch it early.

Get this mental model solid and hoisting, the Temporal Dead Zone, and the `var`-in-a-loop bug stop being memorized trivia and become predictable consequences of one mechanism.

slides.subTitle: Global, function, eval
slides.markdown:
JavaScript creates an execution context every time it starts running code in a new environment. There are three kinds:

- **Global context** — created once, when the script starts. Its variable object is the global object (`window` in browsers, `global`/`globalThis` in Node).
- **Function context** — created fresh **every time a function is called**, not every time it's defined. Ten calls to the same function make ten separate contexts, each with its own variables and its own `this`.
- **Eval context** — created when code runs inside `eval()`. It behaves like function or global scope depending on where `eval` was called from, and its variables can leak into the surrounding scope, which is one of several reasons `eval` is avoided in real code.

Contexts stack: calling a function pushes a new context onto the **call stack**, on top of whichever context called it. Returning pops it back off.

slides.subTitle: How a name lookup resolves
slides.markdown:
Every context is linked to the context that lexically **contains** it — the function's outer scope, not whoever called it. That chain of links is the **scope chain**.

When your code reads a variable, the engine walks the chain: check the current context's variables, and if not found, check the next one out, and the next, until it either finds a binding or reaches global scope and throws a `ReferenceError`.

Crucially, this chain is fixed by **where a function is written**, not where it's called from — that's what "lexical scoping" means. A function defined at the top of a file always looks up through the scopes visible at that location, no matter which deeply-nested call site eventually invokes it. This is also the exact mechanism a **closure** relies on, which the next topic builds on directly.

slides.sectionTitle: How a context is actually built
slides.subTitle: Creation phase, then execution phase
slides.markdown:
Every execution context is built in **two passes**, and almost every hoisting question is really a question about the first one:

1. **Creation phase** — before any line runs, the engine scans the code and allocates memory for every `var` and function declaration (initialized to `undefined` and the actual function respectively), plus every `let`/`const` (left **uninitialized** — not even `undefined`).
2. **Execution phase** — the code runs top to bottom, line by line, now assigning real values into the slots the creation phase already reserved.

So "hoisting" isn't code moving anywhere; it's the creation phase pre-scanning and reserving space ahead of time. What differs between `var` and `let` is only what that reserved slot holds until the execution phase reaches it: `undefined`, or nothing accessible at all.

slides.subTitle: Declarations, never assignments
slides.markdown:
"Hoisting" is the name for the visible effect of the creation phase: it looks like declarations moved to the top of their scope. What actually happens is narrower than most people assume:

- **The declaration** is hoisted — the engine already knows the name exists.
- **The assignment is not.** `var x = 5;` hoists `var x;` (initialized to `undefined`), but the `= 5` stays exactly where it's written and runs only when execution reaches that line.

So this compiles and runs, printing `undefined`, not an error:

```javascript
console.log(x); // undefined — declaration hoisted, assignment hasn't run yet
var x = 5;
```

Function **declarations** hoist their entire body, so you can call one before its line in the source. Function **expressions** (`const f = function() {}`) only hoist the variable, not the function — calling `f()` early throws or fails exactly like any other `var`/`let` misuse.

slides.subTitle: Function scope vs block scope
slides.markdown:
The practical difference candidates need to state precisely:

| | `var` | `let` / `const` |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope unit** | nearest function (or global) | nearest block `{ }` |
| **Creation-phase value** | `undefined` | uninitialized (TDZ) |
| **Redeclaration** | allowed, silently | `SyntaxError` |
| **Attaches to** | `window` at global scope | not attached to `window` |

The scope-unit row is the one that causes real bugs: `var` ignores `if`, `for`, and `{ }` blocks entirely — a `var` declared inside an `if` block is visible for the whole enclosing function. `let`/`const` respect the block, so a variable declared inside a `for` loop's body doesn't leak past its closing brace. That single difference is why the classic loop-closure bug (next slide) exists at all.

slides.subTitle: Why `let`/`const` throw before their line runs
slides.markdown:
`let` and `const` are hoisted too — the creation phase reserves their slot just like `var` — but the slot stays **uninitialized** from the top of the block until execution actually reaches the declaration. That window is the **Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)**.

Touch the name anywhere inside the TDZ and you get a `ReferenceError`, not `undefined`:

```javascript
console.log(a); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'a' before initialization
let a = 10;
```

This is a deliberate design choice, not a bug: the TDZ turns a whole class of "used before assigned" mistakes that `var` silently hides as `undefined` into a hard, immediate crash at the exact line that's wrong. It's stricter than `var`, and that strictness is the point.

slides.subTitle: `var` vs `let` in a `for` loop

slides.sectionTitle: Global scope pollution in the browser
slides.markdown:
At global scope, `var x = 1;` does something `let x = 1;` doesn't: it creates `window.x`, because the browser's global object **is** the global execution context's variable object. Any script on the page, from any `<script>` tag, shares that one `window`.

This is how two unrelated third-party scripts silently clobber each other's `var config = {...}` if they happen to pick the same name — there's exactly one global slot for it. `let`/`const` at the top level still create genuinely global bindings, but deliberately **don't** attach to `window`, which is why modern code wraps everything in modules or IIFEs and reaches for `let`/`const` at the top level instead of bare `var`.

slides.subTitle: A conflict most people never notice
slides.markdown:
Function declarations don't just hoist their name — they hoist their **entire body**, ahead of `var` in the same scope. That creates an ordering trap when a name is used both ways:

```javascript
console.log(typeof greet); // "function", not "undefined"
var greet = "hi";
function greet() {}
```

During the creation phase, the function declaration is processed and installs the full function first; the `var greet` declaration for the same name is then a no-op (it's already declared), so nothing overwrites it yet. Only when execution reaches `var greet = "hi";` does the string assignment finally run and stomp the function.

The senior-level takeaway: hoisting isn't one rule, it's a **priority order** — function declarations first, then `var`, then `let`/`const` reserved-but-uninitialized. Relying on that order in real code is a bug waiting to happen; naming a function and a variable the same thing is the actual fix.

A complete answer to "what is hoisting" has three parts, and most candidates only give the first:

1. **The mechanism** — the creation phase pre-scans a scope and reserves memory for every declaration before any line executes.
2. **What differs by keyword** — `var` and function declarations get real initial values; `let`/`const` get a reserved-but-inaccessible slot (the TDZ).
3. **Why it matters in practice** — it explains `console.log(x); var x` giving `undefined` instead of a crash, why `let` in a `for` loop gives each closure its own value, and why global `var` pollutes `window` while `let` doesn't.

The next topic, closures, builds directly on the scope chain from this one — a closure is nothing more than a function that keeps a live link to an outer context's variables after that context would otherwise have been discarded.
